title: True are His devotees
hook: those who live in truth become true (Sukhmani 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday, dargah: the true court, and a world where truth is the grain of everything. Today, what truth does to people.

Spend a summer with someone who has a strong accent and you'll come home with a little of it. Live with a person who's always on time and you start, grudgingly, to be on time. We take on the shape of what we're near. Parents notice it with their kids' friends; managers notice it with teams. Gurbani has an old picture for this, about a stone and a piece of iron. And the seventeenth ashtpadi has a line that points the same way.
screen: `A SUMMER, AND YOU COME HOME WITH AN ACCENT.` → `WE TAKE THE SHAPE OF WHAT WE'RE NEAR.` → `A STONE AND A PIECE OF IRON.`

segments.voice: Look at yesterday's stanza again. Every line had two halves. True are His feet, and true the one who touches them. True His worship, and true the one who serves. True the Name, and true the one who remembers it. The second half is always a person. The stanza ends, in paraphrase: for the one who understands, everything becomes true. So the truth doesn't stay with God. It spreads to whoever comes near it. The devotee, the bhagat, isn't true by birth, or by being clever about truth. They become true by touching what's true, again and again. Gurbani's picture for this is the paras, the philosopher's stone of Indian legend, which turns iron into gold just by touching it. Gurbani calls the Guru a paras, and Sikhs say the same of the sangat, the company of the good. You don't become gold by thinking about gold. You become gold by contact. That makes truth practical. It isn't mainly an argument you win; it's a substance you're near, or not. In Sikh life, one way people stay near it is small, repeated faithfulness: the morning banis, said every day; the word kept; the promise honored when it's inconvenient. Every kept promise is a little contact with the true. In this picture, nobody becomes true in one heroic act. It happens the way iron becomes gold in the old story: touch by touch.
screen: `TRUE THING, TRUE PERSON: EACH LINE.` · `BHAGAT: THE DEVOTEE.` · `PARAS: IRON TURNED TO GOLD.` · `A KEPT PROMISE IS CONTACT.` · then, large: `BECOME TRUE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the week for one small promise you made and haven't kept yet: a call, a returned book, a 'let's get coffee' you didn't mean. Picture yourself keeping it, simply, without announcing it, as a kind of touch, contact with what's true. If you pray, say Waheguru as you decide.
Paras, the legendary stone that turns iron to gold. The bhagat becomes true by touching the true, like iron turned to gold: touch by touch.
Your line: become true. Iron doesn't turn to gold by thinking about gold. Rest well.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's seventeenth ashtpadi hear each true thing paired with the person who meets it, and Gurbani calls the Guru a paras, the stone that turns iron to gold.

chat.says: How does a person actually become truthful? Do you just decide one day?
options: Gurbani's picture is the paras: you become true by contact, touch by touch, like kept promises.
Yes, one big honest act is enough; after that, truthfulness is simply who you are.
Devotees are born true; the rest of us can only admire them from a distance.
chat.meaning: The stanza pairs every true thing with a person who meets it. Like iron near the paras, people become true by repeated contact with the true.
